opening.headline: We solve the invisible problem of where LLM calls are slow using logs, metrics, traces, context propagation, and GenAI semantic protocols.
body: The user says the response took 8 seconds. However, the server log records only the start and end times of the request. If you don't know what's slow - searching, assembling prompts, calling models, or running tools - improvement becomes guesswork.

In this lesson, we'll start by looking at what observability is and what logs, metrics, and traces show. Next, we read context propagation that connects a single request across service boundaries and the W3C Trace Context, and look at the GenAI semantic convention that sets standard names for properties contained in LLM call spans. At the end, we explain an example of decomposing a slow request into a trace and finding the cause of the trace being interrupted.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain logs, metrics, traces and context propagation
You can distinguish which questions the properties of the GenAI semantic convention answer.
Explains the difference between the head and tail methods of trace sampling, and allows you to distinguish between broken traces and traces that did not remain through sampling.

screens.title: I don't see where the LLM call is slowing down
screens.lead: Select the hidden sections in the picture one by one and check the time each section might have taken and why you cannot tell with the log you have now.

visual.alt: The 8-second interval between the start and end of the request can be divided into search, prompt assembly, model call, and tool execution, but the picture is obscured by a question mark.

items.prompt: User: It took 8 seconds to respond
items.answer: The delay perceived by the user is 8 seconds, but the user does not know at what stage this number was created. The problem is also difficult to reproduce. If you send the same request again, this time it may take 2 seconds.

items.prompt: Server log: only the beginning and end are stamped
items.answer: The log only contains the time the request came in and went out. What happened in the meantime is not recorded. Logs are just time stamped messages and are not guaranteed to be linked to a specific request.

items.prompt: Hidden sections: search, assemble prompts, call models, run tools
items.answer: It is not clear which of the four stages the request goes through is slow. If the model call is slow, it may be a model-side issue, and if the tool execution is slow, it may be an external system issue. The direction of improvement is exactly the opposite.

items.prompt: Conclusion: We need a way to look inside the system from the outside.
items.answer: The application should be able to emit signals on its own so that the cause can be determined without additional work after the fact. This property is observable.

screens.outro: Now that we have confirmed the shape of the obscured section, let us recall a similar experience.

screens.title: Think back: The night I searched through the logs
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: I can't see where the LLM call is slowing down. Have you ever seen a similar situation?
items.answer: If you receive a complaint that it's slow, but you can't tell which step it's due to, it's the same situation. If this situation is repeated, the team will make speculative improvements such as changing the model or adding cache without any basis.

items.prompt: Have you ever tried to track a single request by sorting logs from multiple services in chronological order?
items.answer: When a single request passes through multiple services, it ends up scattered in their respective logs. Following this visually is slow and easy to make mistakes. If the requests are tagged with a common identifier, this is a single search.

items.prompt: Has there ever been a situation where the user was unable to do what he/she wanted even though the service was up?
items.answer: The fact that it's up and running is different from the fact that it's working as users expect. As in the example in the OpenTelemetry article, even if the system is running 100%, if the wrong product is added to the shopping cart, the system is unreliable. This is a case where a response is received from the AI ​​service, but the content is incorrect.

screens.outro: First, let us summarize the concept of observability.

screens.title: Observability Concept: Asking from the outside what is happening inside
screens.lead: The following flashcards illustrate five concepts needed to understand observability. When you select a card, it flips over. Select the right arrow to go to the next card.

cards.back: Even if you don't know the internal structure, you can understand the cause by asking questions through the output of the system. The key is to be able to deal with unexpected problems - problems where you don't know in advance what questions to ask. Your system is well-instrumented if you already have the information you need without having to add more code to solve the problem.

The task of causing application code to emit a signal. OpenTelemetry is a means of making systems observable by instrumenting application code. Areas where no signal is coming out will not be visible no matter how many times you change the tool.

This is the answer to the question: Is the service performing as expected by the user? You can't judge based on uptime alone. Even if a system is always up, it can't be trusted if it doesn't do exactly what the user asks it to do.

It is an aggregate of numerical data from an infrastructure or application over a certain period of time. Examples include system error rate, CPU utilization, and request rate by service. For AI services, this includes values ​​such as response delay, token usage, and error rate.

SLI is a measurement of the behavior of a service from the user's perspective, such as the speed at which a web page loads. SLOs are goals that convey credibility to an organization or other teams by linking one or more SLIs to business value. For example, the percentage of requests that come in within the LLM response delay time is the SLI.

screens.outro: Now that we've organized the concepts, let's compare the types of signals one by one.

screens.title: Signals: logs, metrics, traces
screens.lead: Select each tab to compare what the same slow LLM call looks like in logs, metrics, and traces.

visual.alt: A side-by-side diagram showing how one request is recorded in three different signals: log, metrics, and trace.

tabs.label: What is a signal?
tabs.body: Signals are system outputs that describe the activity of the operating system and applications running on the platform. The purpose of OpenTelemetry is to collect, process, and emit these signals. The signals that OpenTelemetry handles are traces, metrics, logs, and baggage. Multiple signals are used together to view the internals of the same technology from different angles.

tabs.label: log
tabs.body: Logs are time-stamped messages emitted by a service or component. Unlike traces, there is no guarantee that they are linked to a specific request or transaction. In your application, when you turn on auto-instrumentation or the SDK for logs created by any logging library, OpenTelemetry automatically associates them with active traces and spans and assigns IDs to the logs. If multiple requests are mixed at the same time, it is difficult to determine which log is the slow call.

tabs.label: metric
tabs.body: Metrics are aggregates of values measured at runtime. Slow calls manifest themselves in the form of increased average or upper percentile delays. This is good for determining whether everything or only a specific path is slow, but it is impossible to tell which section of an individual request is slow through metrics alone.

tabs.label: trace
tabs.body: A trace is the path a request took through the system. A trace is made up of spans, and a span is a unit of work and has a name, start and end times, and properties. Slow calls show interval times, with the model call spanning, say, 6 seconds. Distributed tracing lets you observe the propagation of requests in complex distributed systems and debug behavior that is difficult to reproduce locally.

tabs.label: relationship between signals
tabs.body: The three signs are not in competition but rather complement each other. Metrics signal that there is a problem, traces show you which section, and logs tell you what happened within that section. Logs become much more useful when connected to spans or traces.

screens.outro: To bundle signals into a single request, context must be passed between services. Next, let's look at context propagation.

screens.title: Context propagation and Trace Context
screens.lead: Below is an example traceparent header from the OpenTelemetry documentation. Select the underlined passage to see what each field means.

data.text:
traceparent: 00-a0892f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-f03067aa0ba902b7-01

Fields: <version>-<trace-id>-<parent-id>-<trace-flags>
Call flow: Frontend (calling side) -> Product Catalog (receiving side)

marks.note: The first field is the version. Indicates the version of the header format defined by the W3C Trace Context specification.

The second field is Trace ID. This is a value that identifies the entire request, and remains the same no matter how many services it passes through. If this value is added to the log, logs from different services can be collected in one request.

The third field is the parent ID, i.e. the ID of the calling span. Since the receiving side uses this value as the parent of its own span, the spans of the two services are connected as parents and children.

The fourth field is the trace flags. It is an eight-bit value, and if the rightmost bit (sampled) is on, it means that the caller may be recording data for this trace. 01 is the value where only the sampled bit is turned on. This value is a hint rather than a strict command, so the recipient may judge it differently depending on their own circumstances. Learn more about what sampling is in the next screen.

marks.span: Call flow: Frontend (calling side) -> Product Catalog (receiving side)
marks.note: When Frontend calls Product Catalog, Frontend sends the Trace ID and Span ID in the context to the traceparent header. Product Catalog creates a new span belonging to the same trace with this value and sets the span in Frontend as its parent. OpenTelemetry's default propagation method is the W3C TraceContext header. This tracks the entire flow of requests across service boundaries.

screens.outro: Now that we have confirmed the meaning of the header, we will now look at the principle of sampling, which leaves only a portion of the trace rather than all of it.

screens.title: Trace Sampling: Why and How to Leave Not All Traces
screens.lead: Select the right arrow to step through the steps to see where sampling decisions are made, how they are propagated to sub-services, and what the head and tail approaches miss.

steps.title: Why leave only some
steps.body: Storing the entire span for each request increases transmission and storage costs proportional to the number of requests. Sampling is a method of processing and exporting only a portion of a trace and discarding the rest, reducing costs while maintaining representativeness of the entire trace. Traces that have been processed and exported are called sampled, and traces that have not been processed are called not sampled. In particular, LLM calls create multiple spans at once and the input and output contents tend to be large, resulting in a large storage burden.

steps.title: Decision made once, propagated through header
steps.body: If the sampling decisions for a request are different across services, some of the spans of the same trace will remain, creating holes. So, the one that makes the decision first sends the result to the sampled bit in the trace flag of the traceparent, and the lower level service continues the same decision according to this value. However, this bit is only a hint, allowing subservices with high load to reduce more aggressively.

steps.title: Head Sampling: Decide When You Start
steps.body: Head sampling determines whether to leave the entire trace at the beginning of the request. A typical method is probability-based sampling, which is determined by a Trace ID and a target percentage (e.g. 5%). Since the decision is calculated from the Trace ID, the results are the same for each service. It's simple, efficient, and can be used at any point in the pipeline. The limitation is that we don't know what hasn't happened yet. There is no guarantee that an error trace will be left, as we don't know if this request will result in an error later or if it will take as long as 8 seconds.

steps.title: Tail Sampling: Decide after completion
steps.body: Tail sampling is determined by looking at the entire trace after most of its spans have been collected. You can use rules such as always leaving traces containing errors, leaving when the total delay exceeds a standard, leaving more traces with a specific attribute value, so it is suitable for selecting and leaving the slow calls and failed calls that you want to see most in LLM operations. Instead, the spans of one trace must be gathered in one place and held until judgment is completed, so stateful components and resources are needed, and rules must be modified every time the system changes. If the throughput is very large, the two can be used together, such as reducing it first with head sampling and applying tail sampling right before export.

steps.title: Distinguish between broken traces and missing traces
steps.body: The two appear similar but have different causes. When context propagation is lost, a request appears to be split into multiple pieces with different Trace IDs, each of which is stored. If it is not sampled, there is only one Trace ID, and the trace is missing or completely present. If there is a Trace ID in the server log, try searching the backend with that value. If multiple fragments come up, it's a propagation problem, if nothing comes up, I question my sampling decision. In environments with low sampling rates, not seeing certain requests is not an error, but rather a behavior by design.

screens.outro: Now that we know the principles of sampling, let's look at the attribute conventions specific to LLM calls.

screens.title: GenAI semantic conventions: standard names for span properties
screens.lead: Read the table to see which questions each attribute in the LLM call span and tool call span answers. Property names and definitions are based on the OpenTelemetry GenAI convention, and product implementation examples are taken from the spans exported by Claude Code.

data.caption: GenAI protocol properties and questions to answer
rows: gen_ai.operation.name

The type of work performed. There are set values such as chat, text_completion, embeddings, retrieval, and execute_tool, and if there is a corresponding value, the convention determines that that value should be used.
What kind of work is this span?
gen_ai.provider.name

This is an attribute that distinguishes providers. If the value is different, the provider-specific property is attached together, which serves as a standard for distinguishing between telemetry types.
Which supplier's model is it called?
gen_ai.request.model
The name of the requested model. If the model is provided by the supplier, write the exact name requested
Which model did you call it from?
gen_ai.usage.input_tokens
Number of input tokens. The convention recommends containing all types of input tokens, including cached tokens. Claude Code does not set this property directly
Was the input louder than usual?
gen_ai.response.finish_reasons
This is the reason why the model stopped generating the model as a string array.
Was the response completed normally or truncated due to length restrictions?
gen_ai.response.id
ID that identifies the response (Claude Code is the same value as the request ID)
Can you compare records with the supplier?
gen_ai.tool.call.id
The tool call identifier given by the model, recorded in the tool execution span (same value as tool_use_id in Claude Code)
Which tool call is associated with this span
data.notes: A semantic convention is a promise that all tools will record the same meaning as properties with the same name. GenAI protocols are managed in a separate repository and define the spans, metrics, and events of the protocols for each GenAI client, MCP, and provider. The name of the inference span is a concatenation of the task name and the request model, the default type is CLIENT, and the default tool execution span is INTERNAL. Properties that contain content such as user input messages, model output messages, system directives, and tool definitions are classified as opt-in, and the protocol warns that these properties may contain sensitive information, such as personal information. So, the rule is not to record by default and to turn it on when needed. Property names may vary between implementations. For example, Claude Code always records the provider as anthropic in the gen_ai.system property rather than gen_ai.provider.name, so you need to get into the habit of comparing the name in the convention with the name used by the tool. Also, Claude Code does not set the gen_ai.usage.* property directly, so if this value is needed, input_tokens, cache_read_tokens, and cache_creation_tokens must be added and mapped according to the convention. Claude Code's traces are turned off by default and must be turned on by setting CLAUDE_CODE_ENHANCED_TELEMETRY_BETA=1 and OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER.

screens.outro: Now let's move on to an example, decomposing a slow request into a trace.

ext.title: OpenTelemetry GenAI Semantic Conventions (client spans, inference, execute_tool)

screens.title: Commentary 1: Decomposing slow requests into traces
screens.lead: We decompose one request that took 8 seconds to respond (this is a hypothetical numerical example) into a trace. Select the right arrow to follow the waterfall as it is drawn step by step.

steps.title: Step 1: Determine Total Time from Root Span
steps.body: Notice the full 8 seconds in the root span of the trace and expand the subspans. At this point, it is not known which section is the bottleneck. We also check whether the time sum of the subspans is close to the root and whether there is empty time between spans.

steps.title: Step 2: Compare times of subspans
steps.body: The span is divided into 0.4 seconds of search, 0.1 seconds of prompt assembly, 6.5 seconds of model call, and 1 second of tool execution. Total is 8 seconds. The model call span is the majority of the total, so the candidate bottleneck is the model call.

steps.title: Step 3: Narrow down the cause by attribute
steps.body: Look at the `gen_ai.request.model` and Input Token Count attributes of the model call span (the convention name is `gen_ai.usage.input_tokens`). If the model name is the same as usual, but the number of input tokens is much larger than usual, it doesn't mean that the model is slow, but that the input is large. Even for the same model, if the input is large, the processing time increases.

steps.title: Step 4: Determine the reason for termination
steps.body: We also see that `gen_ai.response.finish_reasons` has ended up with a length limit. If you end up with a length limit like max_tokens, the response may be long and take time.

steps.title: Instructor's Conclusion
steps.body: The bottleneck was not the model itself, but the unusually long inputs. A proper improvement would be to reduce the input length instead of changing the model. Without the trace, we might have made the wrong decision to change the model.

screens.outro: Next, we will solve the problem of the trace being cut off in the middle.

screens.title: Explanation 2: Context propagation is the cause of trace interruption
screens.lead: This is a situation where the gateway span and model service span appear as different traces. Select the right arrow to follow the inspection sequence.

steps.title: situation
steps.body: The request initiated by the gateway calls the model service, and the two spans appear as different traces in the trace screen. They're the same request, but they're not connected together, so you can't see the overall delay at a glance.

steps.title: Step 1: Compare Trace IDs
steps.body: Check whether the Trace IDs of the two spans are different. If it is different, it means that the context was not conveyed, and if it is the same but only the parent relationship is misaligned, it is a different type of problem. Compare these values ​​first before suspecting a bug in the tool. Conversely, if one span is not visible at all, first suspect sampling. If a span with the same Trace ID is not stored on either side, it is not broken, but rather left behind due to a sampling decision.

steps.title: Step 2: Does the caller emit headers?
steps.body: Check whether the calling party sends the `traceparent` header in the request. Context propagation is usually handled transparently to the user by the instrumentation library, but custom HTTP clients or asynchronous operations may require you to pass the context manually.

steps.title: Step 3: Check the middle section and the receiving end
steps.body: Check whether an intermediate proxy or queue discards the header, or whether the recipient extracts the context from the header and uses it as the parent of its own span. If the receiving end doesn't read the header, it starts a new trace.

steps.title: Instructor's Conclusion
steps.body: If an injection or extraction is missed for even one section, the subsequent span becomes a new trace. Broken traces are usually a problem with the propagation settings, not a defect in the tool. Find the broken point and check the injection and extraction in that section first.

screens.outro: In the final commentary, we'll look at how to tie logs and metrics to traces.

screens.title: Commentary 3: Binding logs and metrics to traces
screens.lead: Switch between the two states to compare how the same logs and metrics are grouped by request.

states.label: If there is no Trace ID
states.body: If there is no Trace ID in the log, you have to track each request by visually matching the scattered logs for each service. If there are hundreds of requests at the same time, it is difficult to tell which log belongs to which request. Metrics only show the overall average delay, making it difficult to tell which path is slow. SLI can be defined as a response delay from the user's perspective, but it does not lead to traceability.

states.label: If you have a Trace ID
states.body: If a Trace ID is attached to the log, you can select only the warning logs that occurred within the slow span. Logs of the same request can be collected across services at once, and metrics can be aggregated by dividing the delay by call path combination as well as the overall average. If you set SLI as the response delay from the user's perspective and SLO as the target, you can jump straight to the trace of off-target requests. Tools like Claude Code can export metrics and events to the collector as OpenTelemetry environment variables like `CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY`.

screens.outro: I will summarize the key points by grouping the three cases into one.

screens.title: Key takeaway: How to make invisible sections visible
screens.lead: We will organize what we have seen so far into one standard.

paragraphs: Observability is the property of being able to find the cause within a system by asking questions outside of it. This requires that the application be instrumented to emit a signal, and reliability is measured by whether it behaves as users expect, not by uptime.
Log, metric, and trace are the primary signals, and span is the unit of trace. Metrics tell you there is a problem, traces tell you which section it is, and logs tell you what happened in it.

Context propagation uses the traceparent header of the W3C Trace Context to pass the Trace ID and parent ID between services to form a single trace. The GenAI semantic convention standardizes attribute names across LLM call spans, allowing queries and dashboards to be reused even when tools change.
If the trace is broken, first suspect injection and extraction of the propagation header. If a request takes 8 seconds, the first question is to see what spans those 8 seconds are divided into.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: The signal is only visible as measured. Leaving model call spans and their properties with standard names from the beginning allows you to answer questions right away in moments of slowdown.

screens.outro: Finally, let's read an example of a real-world collection setup.

screens.title: Read collection settings: OpenTelemetry environment variable
screens.lead: Below is an example setup to export Claude Code's telemetry to the OpenTelemetry collector. Select a line range from the description on the right to see the symptoms when what each setting does is out of sync.

data.code:
export CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY=1
export OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER=otlp
export OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER=otlp
export OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL=grpc
export OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=http://localhost:4317
export OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS="Authorization=Bearer your-token"
export OTEL_METRIC_EXPORT_INTERVAL=10000
export OTEL_LOGS_EXPORT_INTERVAL=5000
claude

notes.note: This is the switch that turns on telemetry. Without this value, nothing will be exported even if the remaining settings are present. If no signal arrives at the collector after setup, check this value first.
Decide how to export metrics and logs. otlp is sent to the OTLP collector, and there are other options such as console or none. If you set only one side, only that signal will arrive.

OTLP protocol, collector address, authentication header. Claude Code does not have a default protocol, so you must specify a protocol to use otlp export. If the address or protocol is incorrect, the signal will be lost due to a connection error, and if the header is incorrect, the collector will reject the request.

This is the export cycle. The metric default is 60000 ms and the log default is 5000 ms, here we have reduced the metric to 10 seconds to make it easier to verify the settings. In operation, return it to default.
After completing the settings, run Claude Code. If your setup emits metrics, ensure that the claude_code.session.count metric created when the session starts is visible to the collection backend.

glossary.def: This is the property of being able to question and understand the internal state of a system through external output.
A unit of work is recorded with name, time, and attributes.
The path the request took through the system. It consists of a set of spans.
This involves connecting spans into a single trace by passing the Trace ID and parent Span ID across the service boundary.
A promise to standardize property names for spans, metrics, and events in generative AI operations such as LLM calls.

This method reduces costs by processing and exporting only part of the trace. There is a head method, which is determined at the beginning, and a tail method, which is determined after looking at the entire trace.

misconceptions.myth: Observability can be secured by leaving enough logs.
misconceptions.fact: Logs that are not connected to the request have limitations in tracing the cause. Logs must be associated with traces, and metrics and traces must exist together.

misconceptions.myth: If a service is up and running, you can trust it.
misconceptions.fact: Reliability is a matter of whether the service performs as users expect. Even if you have 100% uptime, you can't trust it if it doesn't do what your users ask it to do.

misconceptions.myth: The trace being cut off is a bug in the observation tool.
misconceptions.fact: This is usually caused by missing header injection or extraction during context propagation. This can also be caused by the proxy or queue not forwarding the headers.

misconceptions.myth: If the trace is not visible, context propagation has been interrupted.
misconceptions.fact: Disconnection and sampling are different. If the radio wave is cut off, the same request appears divided into different Trace IDs, and if it is not sampled, there will be no trace for that Trace ID at all.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Observability is the property of being able to find the cause by asking questions from the outside.
Logs, metrics, traces and spans are the basic concepts.
Context propagation stitches requests between services into a single trace.
The GenAI semantic convention standardizes attribute names in LLM call spans.
Sampling is a sparing method, and requires tail-wise rules to avoid missing errors and slow calls.
